<pasted_content id="cfee">
You are helping me complete the Eneba Intern Assignment 2027 (the PDF is in this folder). Read it fully first. 
The deadline is 7 days. A key requirement: the FULL agent chat history (prompts + responses) must be submitted, 
and they evaluate HOW I use AI. I must be able to explain every line of code and every decision.

Work in phases. Do NOT write any application code in this session — this session is setup, research and planning only. NEVER push or merge anything. ONLY do the tasks you were told to do.

## Phase 1 — Logging (do this FIRST, before anything else)
Goal: every Claude Code session in this project (including subagents) is automatically saved into the repo, 
complete and readable, starting with THIS session.

1. Initialize git here and set remote origin to https://github.com/Jokubas-J/Eneba.git
2. Create a Node script `.claude/hooks/export-log.mjs` (no external dependencies) that:
   - reads the hook JSON from stdin (uses `transcript_path`, `session_id`, and `agent_transcript_path` for subagents)
   - copies the JSONL transcript to `ai-logs/raw/<session_id>.jsonl` (and subagents to `ai-logs/raw/subagents/`), 
     with any thinking/reasoning blocks removed
   - renders a readable Markdown version to `ai-logs/<date>_<session_id>.md`: every user prompt, every assistant 
     response (visible text only, no thinking/reasoning blocks), and every tool call with its input and a 
     truncated result
   - redacts secrets (Stripe keys sk_/pk_/whsec_, JWT secrets, DB connection string passwords, anything from .env) 
     in BOTH the raw copy and the markdown
   - never fails loudly (exit 0 on errors, write errors to `ai-logs/hook-errors.log`)
3. Register it in `.claude/settings.json` (project-level, committed) on the Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact and 
   SessionEnd events. I am on Windows — make sure the command works there (use "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" and `node`).
4. Test it: run the script manually with this session's real transcript path so this session is backfilled 
   from the very first prompt. Show me the generated markdown file path and the first lines of it.
5. Tell me clearly if hooks require me to restart Claude Code or approve them in /hooks to become active.
6. Create `ai-logs/README.md` explaining how logs are produced, so the evaluators understand the folder.

## Phase 2 — Analyse the task
- Break down every requirement from the PDF into an explicit checklist (functional, technical, deliverables).
- Note where the spec is vague and list the interpretation options for each.

## Phase 3 — Study eneba.com
- Inspect eneba.com (homepage, store/catalog with filters, search, a product page with multiple seller offers, 
  cart/checkout flow as far as possible without paying). If plain fetching is blocked (Cloudflare), install and use 
  the Playwright MCP to browse and take screenshots.
- Extract a design reference into `docs/design-reference.md`: color palette (hex values), typography (fonts, sizes, 
  weights), spacing, border radius, shadows, key components (header, search bar, product card, offer row, buttons, 
  badges, filters sidebar, footer). Save screenshots to `docs/screenshots/`.
- Describe how Eneba's data model seems to work (products vs offers vs sellers, platforms, regions).

## Phase 4 — Research the best approach (use web search)
Constraints: React (TypeScript), backend in Go or PHP, REST or GraphQL, any DB, free-tier deployment.
Research and compare, with sources:
- Backend: Go vs PHP for this. I know C/C++ and C# better than TS — readability and explainability matter.
- Database + typo-tolerant search (e.g. Postgres pg_trgm vs Meilisearch/Typesense vs others) — cost, free-tier fit.
- Payments in test mode (e.g. Stripe test mode + webhooks) and safe digital key delivery (no double-selling).
- Auth approach (sessions vs JWT, httpOnly cookies).
- Homepage requirement: "each block gets its content from its own backend service or database" — how to satisfy 
  this sensibly without over-engineering.
- Free hosting for frontend, backend and DB in late 2026 (limits, cold starts, which combos work together).
Separate facts from your opinions. Recommend one option per decision with the reasoning.

## Phase 5 — Tools: skills, plugins, agents, MCPs
- Search for Claude Code skills, plugins, subagents and MCP servers that would genuinely help with this project 
  (e.g. frontend design, Playwright/browser testing, Go/React best practices, code review, testing).
- Prefer official Anthropic / well-known, widely used sources. For every third-party one, check what it runs and 
  whether it is maintained. Do not install anything that looks untrustworthy.
- Install the useful ones at project level where possible. List each one in `docs/tooling.md` with: what it is, 
  source link, why I chose it, how I will use it.

## Phase 6 — Plan
Write `PLAN.md` containing:
- Scope decision: which 2–3 features to go deep on and which to keep minimal, with justification 
  (the brief says "a few features done extensively beat many fitting minimal requirements")
- Architecture diagram (Mermaid), data model (tables + relations), API endpoint list
- Tech stack with justification for each choice
- Day-by-day plan for 7 days, with deployment set up on day 1
- Risks and fallbacks
- Testing approach
- What the final README must explain (scope choices, trade-offs, how AI was used)

Also create `CLAUDE.md` with the project rules for all future sessions:
- logging must stay enabled; never delete or edit files in ai-logs/
- explain non-trivial code decisions as you go, so I can defend them
- keep commits small with clear messages; you may commit and push to the main branch
- never commit secrets; use .env files with .env.example
- follow docs/design-reference.md for all UI work

## Finish
You should NEVER push or merge. Give me a short summary: what logging is in place and whether I need to restart, the key decisions you recommend, what you installed, and the open questions I need to answer before we start coding.
</pasted_content id="cfee">

content.content:
The pasted page is truncated. Its Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, and SessionEnd input schemas, the workspace trust section, and the subagent transcript details aren't included, so I can't confirm some of what you asked for.

**1. JSON input fields**

The excerpt doesn't include per-event schemas for Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, or SessionEnd, and it never mentions `agent_transcript_path`. The common fields apply to all events:

- `session_id`: "Current session identifier"
- `transcript_path`: "Path to conversation JSON. The transcript file is written asynchronously and may lag the in-memory conversation..."
- `cwd`: "Current working directory when the hook is invoked"
- `agent_id` and `agent_type`: identify the subagent or teammate the hook fires in. `agent_type` is "Present when the session uses `--agent` or the hook fires inside a subagent."

For Stop and SubagentStop, the page says to use `last_assistant_message` instead of reading the transcript for the final assistant text. The field's definition isn't in the excerpt. SessionEnd matcher values are `clear`, `resume`, `logout`, `prompt_input_exit`, and `other`. PreCompact matcher values are `manual` and `auto`.

**2. settings.json format for command hooks**

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "if": "Bash(rm *)",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/block-rm.sh",
            "args": []
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Command handler fields:

- `command`: "Shell command to execute. With `args`, the executable to spawn directly."
- `args`: when present, "`command` is resolved as an executable and spawned directly... with no shell involved."
- `shell`: "Accepts `"bash"` or `"powershell"`. Defaults to `"bash"`, or to `"powershell"` on Windows when Git Bash isn't installed... Ignored when `args` is set."
- `timeout`: "Defaults: 600 for `command`, `http`, and `mcp_tool`; 30 for `prompt`; 60 for `agent`." It is lowered to 30 on UserPromptSubmit, PreModelSwitch, and PostModelSwitch, and to 10 on MessageDisplay.
- `async`: "If `true`, runs in the background without blocking." The page also says "Claude Code doesn't enforce [timeout] on a command hook you run with `async: true`."
- `asyncRewake`: "runs in the background and wakes Claude on exit code 2."
- `once`: "If `true`, Claude Code removes the hook after its first successful run." This is honored only in skill frontmatter.
- `onFailure`: `"continue"` or `"block"`, available in v2.1.295 or later.

**3. Windows and `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`**

- Shell form uses "`sh -c` on macOS and Linux, Git Bash on Windows, or PowerShell when Git Bash isn't installed."
- Exec form on Windows: "`command` to resolve to a real executable such as a `.exe`. The `.cmd` and `.bat` shims... are not executables." For npm-installed tools, the page recommends `"command": "node", "args": [...]`.
- The page's Windows example runs a PowerShell script through the `"shell"`-less exec form:
  ```json
  "command": "powershell.exe",
  "args": ["-NoProfile", "-ExecutionPolicy", "Bypass", "-File", "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/block-rm.ps1"]
  ```
- `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` is "the project root where the session started." It is also exported as an environment variable on the spawned process. "Prefer exec form for any hook that references a path placeholder. In shell form, wrap each placeholder in double quotes."
- Worktrees: `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` keeps pointing at the main project root, while `cwd` in the input JSON follows Claude.

**4. Do edits take effect immediately?**

"Direct edits to hooks in settings files are normally picked up automatically by the file watcher." The excerpt doesn't mention a restart or a review step. The `/hooks` menu is described as "a read-only browser for your configured hooks," so it's for inspection, not approval.

**5. Workspace trust for project hooks**

The excerpt doesn't contain the settings-file trust rule. It links to a "Workspace trust" section that was cut off. Two related statements are in the excerpt:

- For project skill frontmatter: "Frontmatter hooks in a project skill follow the same workspace trust rule as hooks in settings files."
- For project subagent frontmatter: "Frontmatter hooks in a project subagent run only after you accept the workspace trust dialog for the folder the agent file came from. A `-p` session doesn't count as accepting it."

So project-level hooks are subject to a workspace trust rule, but its exact wording isn't in the excerpt.

**6. Subagent transcript storage**

The excerpt doesn't say where subagent transcripts are stored. It only shows the main-session example `/home/user/.claude/projects/.../transcript.jsonl` for `transcript_path`. Check the full page, or the linked subagents documentation, for that path.

input.content:
# AI conversation logs

This folder contains the **full history of every Claude Code session** used to build this project,
as required by the assignment ("agent chat history, full, both prompts and responses").

Nothing here is written by hand. The files are produced automatically by a small script that
Claude Code runs as a *hook*.

## What is in this folder

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `<date>_<session_id>.md` | **Start here.** Readable log of one session: every user prompt, every assistant response, every tool call with its input and a truncated result. |
| `subagents/<date>_<session_id>_<agent>.md` | Same, for subagents (helper agents the main session started). |
| `raw/<session_id>.jsonl` | Machine-readable copy of the same session (one JSON record per line), with untruncated tool results. |
| `raw/subagents/` | Raw copies of subagent transcripts. |
| `hook-errors.log` | Only exists if the export script ever failed; it logs the error instead of interrupting the session. |

The date in a file name is the day the session started. Sessions are listed in chronological order
by file name; a long session that was continued on another day keeps its original file.

## How the logs are produced

1. Claude Code stores each session as a JSONL transcript in the user's home folder
   (`~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session_id>.jsonl`).
2. `.claude/settings.json` (committed in this repo) registers the script
   `.claude/hooks/export-log.mjs` on four hook events:
   - `Stop` — after every assistant turn,
   - `SubagentStop` — when a subagent finishes,
   - `PreCompact` — before a long conversation is compacted,
   - `SessionEnd` — when the session is closed.
3. On each event the script re-reads the **whole** transcript and overwrites the files above with the
   more complete version. There is no incremental state, so a missed event is repaired by the next one.

The script uses only Node.js built-ins (no dependencies). It always exits with code 0, so a logging
problem can never break a coding session.

## What is changed compared to the original transcript

The logs are complete as a conversation record, with these deliberate differences:

- **Model thinking/reasoning blocks are removed** (in both the Markdown and the raw copy). Only the
  visible conversation is kept: prompts, responses, tool calls and tool results.
- **Secrets are redacted** in both formats and replaced with `[REDACTED:...]`: Stripe keys
  (`sk_`, `pk_`, `rk_`, `whsec_`), JWTs, GitHub/Anthropic tokens, passwords inside connection strings,
  `SOMETHING_SECRET=[REDACTED] assignments, and every value found in the project's `.env` files
  (values that also appear in the committed `.env.example` are considered public and kept).
- **Internal bookkeeping records are dropped** from the raw copy (cached API requests, file
  snapshots, account identifiers). Only `user`, `assistant` and `system` records are kept.
- **Embedded binary files** (base64 images/PDFs returned by tools) are replaced with a placeholder.
- In the Markdown only, **tool results are truncated** to 2,000 characters and very long tool inputs
  to 10,000 characters. The raw copy keeps them in full.

Messages that Claude Code itself injected (for example skill instructions or compaction summaries)
are shown in collapsed "injected by Claude Code" blocks so they are not confused with prompts typed
by the user.

## Regenerating the logs manually

```bash
# re-export every session of this project
node .claude/hooks/export-log.mjs --all

# re-export one transcript
node .claude/hooks/export-log.mjs --transcript <path-to-transcript.jsonl>
```

## Known limitations

- `.env` values are redacted using the `.env` files that exist at export time. If a secret is
  rotated mid-session, the old value is only caught by the generic patterns above.
- The transcript is written to disk asynchronously by Claude Code, so the very last message of a
  turn can be missing until the next hook event (at the latest `SessionEnd`) re-exports the session.

input.content:
# Eneba design reference

Extracted from the live site **eneba.com on 2026-11-16** (desktop, 1568 px wide viewport, English EU / EUR,
logged out). Values come from the browser's *computed styles* (read with JavaScript in the page), not
from guessing off screenshots. Screenshots are in [`docs/screenshots/`](screenshots/).

> How to use this file: all UI work must take colors, font sizes, spacing and component shapes from
> here. Where a value is marked *(approx.)* it was estimated from a screenshot rather than measured.

## 1. Overall look

- **Dark, saturated purple everywhere.** There is no white page background; white is only used for
  text, thin outlines and the payment-logo strip.
- **Completely square corners.** Cards, buttons, inputs and panels all have `border-radius: 0`.
  The only rounded things are pill badges (`50px`), checkboxes (`3px`) and one promo nav pill (`5px`).
- **Very bold type.** Almost all UI text is weight 800; body copy is 400.
- **Flat.** Shadows are rare and soft; depth comes from darker/lighter purple panels.
- **One loud accent:** yellow call-to-action buttons with black text.
- Content is centred in a **1200 px** container (1240 px including 20 px side padding).

## 2. Color palette

| Token (suggested name) | Hex | Where Eneba uses it |
|---|---|---|
| `purple-base` | `#4618AC` | Page background (`body`) |
| `purple-light` | `#5825CC` | Raised panels: buy box, category tiles, search dropdown, mobile filter header |
| `purple-dark` | `#351183` | Sunk panels: cart/summary panels, notice box, alternating homepage bands, checkout top bar |
| `purple-deep` | `#1F0A4D` | Product card body, text color on teal badges, inset shadow color |
| `overlay-nav` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.25)` | Nav bar strip under the header |
| `overlay-row` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.30)` | Offer rows on the product page |
| `overlay-input` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.20)` | Inputs/selects background (with inset shadow) |
| `overlay-item` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.12)` | Cart line item |
| `overlay-footer` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.70)` | Footer background (over `purple-base` → almost black-purple) |
| `yellow` | `#FAD318` | Primary buttons (Add to cart, Buy now, Proceed to checkout), "Clear all" link, notice title, "FEATURED OFFER" label |
| `teal` | `#63E3C2` | CASHBACK badge background, product card border |
| `green-region` | `#23C299` | Region label when the key works in the visitor's country; "Cashback deal" pill outline |
| `green-cashback` | `#84E916` | Cashback amounts, discount percent (`-69%`), "Best cashback" pill |
| `pink-region` | `#E76A8C` | Region label when the key is for a different region (warning) |
| `text` | `#FFFFFF` | Main text |
| `text-nav` | `#DCD8E6` | Nav links, footer links |
| `text-muted` | `#B3AAC9` | "From" label, legal text, helper text |
| `text-faded` | `rgba(255,255,255,0.7)` | Filter counts, struck-through old price |
| `black` | `#000000` | Text on yellow buttons |
| `white-strip` | `#FFFFFF` | Payment-methods strip above the footer; PayPal button |
| promo gradient | `linear-gradient(90deg, #D32252 0%, #3C1395 100%)` | Highlighted nav pill ("GTA VI") |

## 3. Typography

- **Font family:** `metropolis, Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif`. Loaded weights: **400, 600, 800**
  (700 is requested for headings and rendered with the nearest loaded weight).
  Metropolis is an open-source font (available e.g. as the `@fontsource/metropolis` npm package),
  so we can use the same typeface legally.
- Base: `16px / 24px`, weight 400, white.

| Element | Size / line-height | Weight | Color |
|---|---|---|---|
| Page title `h1` (store) | 30 / 37.5 px | 700 | white |
| Product title `h1` | 26 / 32.5 px | 700 | white |
| Section heading `h2` (homepage blocks) | 30 / 37.5 px | 700 | white |
| Nav link | 16 / 16 px | 600 | `#DCD8E6` |
| Search input text | 19 / 19 px | 800 | white (placeholder white) |
| Button label | 15 / 15 px | 800 | black on yellow / white on outline |
| Card title | 12 / 18 px | 800 | white (2 lines max, then ellipsis) |
| Card region label | 12 / 12 px | 800, UPPERCASE | green or pink |
| Card "From" | 12 / 12 px | 800 | `#B3AAC9` |
| Card price | 22 / 22 px | 800 | white |
| Card cashback line | 12 / 20 px | 800 | `#84E916` |
| Card platform strip | 10–12 px | 800 | white 85% |
| Buy-box price | 28 / 28 px | 800 | white |
| Offer-row price | 20 / 25 px | 800 | white |
| Old (struck) price | 12 / 18 px | 800 | white 70% |
| Seller name | 14 px | 600 | white |
| Seller rating | 11 px | 800 | white 85% |
| Filter group title | 16 / 22.4 px | 800 | white |
| Filter option / count | 14 px | 400 | white / white 70% |
| Footer column title | 14 / 21 px | 800 | white |
| Footer link | 12 / 18 px | 400 | `#DCD8E6` |
| Legal text | 12 / 18 px | 600 | `#B3AAC9` |
| Tiny label ("FEATURED OFFER") | 10 / 15 px | 800, UPPERCASE | yellow |

## 4. Spacing, radius, shadows

- **Container:** max-width 1200 px, side padding 20 px.
- **Spacing scale seen in the wild:** 5, 10, 15, 20, 40 px (multiples of 5, not 4 or 8).
  - Card text block padding: `15px 15px 10px`
  - Offer row padding: `20px`
  - Button horizontal padding: `10px`; nav link padding: `10px`
  - Homepage sections: `40px` top padding
  - Card gap in carousels/grids: ≈ 20 px *(approx.)*
- **Border radius:** `0` by default. `50px` pills, `3px` checkbox, `5px` promo nav pill.
- **Borders:** 1 px. White for outline buttons and the search box; teal `#63E3C2` around product
  cards; yellow around the notice box.
- **Shadows (only three):**
  - Raised panel (buy box): `0 3px 9px rgba(0,0,0,0.25)`
  - Category tile: `0 7px 15px rgba(0,0,0,0.2)`
  - Input (inset): `inset 0 1px 3px #1F0A4D`

## 5. Components

### Header (screenshot 01)
- Transparent over the purple page, total height ≈ 147 px in two rows:
  1. **Top row (57 px):** logo (left) · search box · language/currency selector with flag
     ("English EU | EUR") · wishlist heart · cart icon (with red count bubble) · "Log in | Register".
  2. **Nav strip (50 px):** background `rgba(0,0,0,0.25)`, full width. "☰ Categories" first, then
     text links (16 px / 600 / `#DCD8E6`), one highlighted promo pill with the pink→purple gradient.
- **Checkout header** is different: logo + 3-step progress bar ("1 Cart — 2 Payment — 3 Get your
  product", active step in teal) on `#351183`, no search or nav (screenshot 14).

### Search bar (screenshots 01, 09)
- 550 × 57 px, transparent, **1 px white border**, no radius. Magnifier icon on the left
  (input has 40 px left padding), clear "✕" on the right when text is present.
- Text 19 px / 800; placeholder "Search for games, top-ups and more" in white.
- **Dropdown** (panel `#5825CC`, same width as the input) has two parts:
  1. up to 5 **query suggestions** (corrected spellings — typing `witchr 3` suggests `witcher 3`,
     `witcher 3 remastered`, …), each with a small magnifier icon;
  2. **product hits**: thumbnail, pill "Digital good", bold title, right-aligned "From ~~€49.99~~" and
     price. The page behind is dimmed.
- Pressing Enter goes to the store with `?text=<query>`.

### Product card (screenshots 02–05)
- ≈ 222 × 456 px, background `#1F0A4D`, **1 px teal border `#63E3C2`**, no radius.
- Top: cover image 222 × 311 px, `object-fit: cover` (portrait, ratio ≈ 5:7).
- Over the image bottom-left: **CASHBACK badge** — teal `#63E3C2`, text `#1F0A4D` 12 px / 800,
  padding `7px 5px`, small icon, height 30 px.
- Directly under it, overlapping the image bottom: **platform strip** — full width, 22 px high,
  `rgba(0,0,0,0.55)`, centred platform icon + name ("Steam", "PSN", "Xbox Live").
- Text block (padding `15px 15px 10px`):
  - title, 2 lines clamp;
  - REGION in uppercase — **green `#23C299`** if usable in your country, **pink `#E76A8C`** if not;
  - "From" + optional ~~old price~~ and `-49%` in green;
  - price 22 px / 800 with a small ⓘ icon;
  - "Cashback: €1.69" in green.
- **Hover:** the image area shrinks, a wishlist heart appears top-right, and two full-width buttons
  slide in at the bottom: yellow **Add to cart** and outline **View offers** (screenshot 03).

### Buttons
| Variant | Background | Text | Border | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | `#FAD318` | black, 15 px / 800 | none | height 35 px, padding `0 10px`, radius 0 |
| Secondary / outline | transparent | white, 15 px / 800 | 1 px white | same |
| "Show all" / "Load more" | outline variant, ≈ 194 × 35 px, centred under a block | | | |
| White (PayPal) | `#FFFFFF` | logo | none | same height |

### Badges
- **CASHBACK** (card): square teal block, see above.
- **Pill outline** ("Cashback deal", "Best cashback", "Digital good"): transparent, 1 px border in
  the text color, radius 50 px, 10–16 px / 800, padding `3px 5px` (small) or `0 12px` (large).
- **Discount** (`-69%`): plain green text `#84E916` next to the struck old price, no background.
- **Cart count:** small red circle on the cart icon.

### Offer row (product page, screenshot 12)
- Full-width row, background `rgba(0,0,0,0.3)`, padding 20 px, ≈ 109 px high, small gap between rows.
- Left: round seller avatar (≈ 40 px), **seller name** (14 px / 600) with a green verified tick,
  below it ★ **rating "9.80"** + "Superb rating" (11 px).
- Right: ~~old price~~ + green `-62%`, **price** 20 px / 800, "11% Cashback" line, then an outline
  **Buy now** button and a small cart-plus icon button.
- Lists: "Recommended offers" (featured offer "Verified by Eneba" first), then
  "**15** other offers" (count in teal), then an outline "Load 12 more offers" button.

### Buy box (product page right column, screenshot 11)
- Panel `#5825CC`, shadow `0 3px 9px rgba(0,0,0,.25)`, ≈ 310 px wide, sticky on the right.
- "FEATURED OFFER" (10 px yellow caps) · ~~€49.99~~ `-69%` · **€15.57** (28 px) · "14% Cashback" +
  "Best cashback" pill · promo countdown text · white PayPal button · yellow **Buy now** + icon-only
  add-to-cart · link "+15 offers from €14.48".
- Under it: "Safe Checkout Guaranteed" panel with payment-method logos.

### Product page top (screenshot 11)
- Breadcrumbs (Store › Categories › Games › GOG Games › title).
- Cover image left (≈ 220 px), title `h1`, then a 2 × 2 grid of **info tiles**, each icon + bold
  title + small text + yellow link: *Region* ("Global — Can be activated in Lithuania"),
  *Platform* ("GOG.com — Activate/redeem on…"), *Digital key* ("Instant delivery"),
  *Instant refunds*. Then "Works on: Windows".
- Screenshot/video strip, a **notice box** (`#351183`, 1 px yellow border, yellow bold title).
- Lower: offers list, "Gamers also viewed", reviews, description, system requirements, languages,
  release date / publisher / developers.

### Filters sidebar (store, screenshots 08, 10)
- 220 px wide column left of the grid. Each group is a panel with a bold title (16 px / 800) and a
  collapse chevron: **Price range (EUR)** (two inputs "min – max"), **Country** (select "All
  countries"), **Product type**, **Operating system**, **Platforms**, **Genres**, **Regions**.
- Options are checkboxes (20 × 20 px, 2 px white-70% border, radius 3 px) with the label left and
  the **result count right** (white 70%). Long groups show 8 options then "292 more"; big groups
  have a small search box inside.
- Inputs/selects: `rgba(0,0,0,0.2)` background, inset shadow, height 40 px, no radius.
- Above the grid: "Results found: **82**" left, "⇅ Popularity: Most popular ⌄" sort dropdown right.
  Sort options: Popularity, Price low→high, Price high→low, Date newest, Date oldest, Alphabet A–Z.
- **Active filters** are shown as dark chips above the results ("Text: witchr 3 ✕") with a yellow
  "Clear all" link. Counts next to each filter update to match the current result set.
- Grid: 4 cards per row beside the sidebar at this width.

### Homepage blocks (screenshots 01–06), in order
1. **Banner mosaic:** one large promo + three smaller tiles, full container width, ≈ 310 px high.
2. **Category icon rail:** horizontally scrollable white line icons with labels (Games, Gaming
   eCards, eGift Cards, E-money, Steam, PSN, Xbox, …) with arrows.
3. **"Recommended for you"**: row of 5 product cards + centred outline "See all".
4. **"Top games"**: carousel of product cards on a darker band (`#351183`), arrows on the sides,
   thin progress bar under it, "Show all".
5. **"Best selling eGift Cards"**: carousel of brand tiles.
6. **"Best selling gift cards"**: card carousel on a darker band.
7. **"Upcoming games"**: card carousel.
8. **"Categories"**: grid of square tiles (`#5825CC`, shadow) — count on top, white icon, name
   (Action 20698, Adventure, Simulation, Strategy, RPG, Indie, FPS/TPS) + "Load more".
- Section headings are `h2` 30 px with a small ⓘ icon; bands alternate `#4618AC` / `#351183`.

### Cart & checkout (screenshots 13–15)
- **Added-to-cart modal:** centred panel `#5825CC`, cart icon with teal tick, "Added to cart",
  "You have **1 item** in your cart", buttons yellow "Continue shopping" + outline "View cart";
  page dimmed behind.
- **Cart page** (`/checkout`): two columns.
  - Left panel "My cart" (`#351183`): line item (`rgba(0,0,0,.12)`) with cover thumbnail,
    "Sold by ⟨seller⟩", product title, "Digital product", quantity stepper `− 1 +`, price, green
    cashback, wishlist and trash icons.
  - Right: "Where to deliver the order?" (email field, "Remember me") and **Summary** panel: yellow
    full-width "Proceed to checkout", "1 product €15.57", "Service fee", **Total** (large), cashback,
    consent checkboxes (yellow when ticked), collapsible "Got discount code?".
- **Empty cart:** ⓘ icon, "Your cart is empty", yellow "Back to Homepage".
- I stopped at the cart: going further needs an e-mail address and a real payment method.

### Footer (screenshot 07)
- White strip with payment logos, then footer on `rgba(0,0,0,0.7)` (reads as near-black purple).
- Link columns: About Eneba · Buy · Help · Community · Business · Follow us (icons) · Download the
  App (store badges) · Trustpilot score.
- Newsletter row: outline input + outline "Subscribe" button; language/currency button on the right.
- Legal line 12 px `#B3AAC9` with underlined links.

## 6. How Eneba's data model appears to work

These are **inferences from the public site**, not documented facts.

- **Product = one sellable variant, not "a game".** The unit shown on a card and given its own URL
  is the combination *title + edition + platform + region*, e.g.
  `/gog-the-witcher-3-wild-hunt-goty-gog-com-key-global`. "The Witcher 3 (Xbox One) Xbox Live Key
  EUROPE" is a separate product with its own page. Search for one game returns many such products.
- **Offer = one seller's price for one product.** A product page lists many offers
  ("+15 offers from €14.48"). Each offer has a seller, a price, an old/reference price (shown as a
  discount %), a cashback %, and flags such as "Featured offer / Verified by Eneba".
  The card's "From €X" is the cheapest offer; the product page promotes one **featured offer** in
  the buy box (not necessarily the cheapest).
- **Seller (merchant):** name, avatar, verified tick, rating out of 10 with a label ("9.80 Superb").
- **The cart holds offers, not products:** the cart line says "Sold by Digital Imperium".
- **Platform** = where the key is redeemed (Steam, GOG.com, Xbox Live, PSN, Nintendo, EA App…),
  separate from **operating system** (Windows / Mac / Linux) which is its own filter.
- **Region** = where the key can be activated (Global, Europe, United States, a single country…).
  The site compares it with the visitor's country and colors it green ("Can be activated in
  Lithuania") or pink.
- **Product type** (Game, DLC, eGift Card, Gaming eCard, Game points, Software, Subscription) and
  **genres** (many per product) are further facets. Every facet shows a live count.
- **Product details:** description, gallery, system requirements, languages, release date,
  publisher, developer, user reviews with sub-ratings, wishlist count.
- **Store/search state lives in the URL** (`/store/all?text=witchr%203`), so results are shareable.
- **Search** tolerates typos (`witchr 3` → 82 Witcher results) and offers query suggestions plus
  instant product hits in a dropdown.
- **Checkout** is a 3-step flow: Cart → Payment → Get your product. Guests can check out with just
  an e-mail on the real site (our assignment instead requires sign-in for checkout).
- **Homepage blocks** are independent curated/computed lists (recommended, top games, best-selling
  gift cards, upcoming, categories with counts), each with its own "show all" link into the store.

- **Core pattern:** One source describes `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` skipping rows another transaction holds, which turns a table into a job queue for competing workers. A DEV Community post adds that it suits finite resources under concurrent load, such as seats, time slots, inventory units, jobs, or coat hangers, which covers one-key-per-row allocation.

- **Atomic claim:** A Kinda Technical article describes nesting the locked select inside an `UPDATE ... WHERE id = (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)`, which claims a job atomically in a single database round trip. This is the usual way to mark a key as sold in one statement.
- **Lock-holding risk:** An older EndpointDev post on parallel inventory access warns about a transaction that locks a record and then aborts without consuming it, so the record stays unavailable until the lock clears. Keep transactions short (or sell via the UPDATE) to avoid this.

The search covered the first half of your question, the Go 1.22 ServeMux and chi comparison. It did not return anything on sqlc, pgx, or GORM, so I can't speak to that part.

**Standard library routing:** Go 1.22 added method matching and wildcards to `net/http`'s router, so a route can be declared directly in its pattern. The Go Blog describes the release as bringing method matching and wildcards to the package's router. Existing patterns still behave as before, so you can adopt the new syntax one route at a time. Wildcards use braces, and a `{name...}` form catches the remainder of a path. Earlier versions treated braces literally, but Go 1.22 uses them for wildcards, and the GODEBUG setting httpmuxgo121 restores the old behavior.

**Limits and trade-offs:** A few sources note where the stdlib falls short. One argues that the compromises made for backward compatibility make the API confusing and error-prone, and the implementation cannot be efficient. Regex-constrained parameters are another gap: chi supports regular expressions to constrain path variables, while ServeMux requires the whole path segment to be the variable. Also, in 1.22, syntactically invalid patterns cause ServeMux.Handle and ServeMux.HandleFunc to panic.

**Standard library vs. chi:** One widely cited view is that the stdlib now covers most typical REST routing, and that chi remains useful for middleware groups, nested routes, and regex constraints. A calhoun.io post that compares the two says its author still prefers chi for most projects, though that is one opinion from 2024, not a consensus. The 2026 sources I found were mostly tutorials that treat stdlib routing as sufficient for ordinary APIs.

**Not covered:** I found nothing on sqlc vs pgx vs GORM. A follow-up search on that topic would be needed.

> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Install and manage plugins

> Install Claude Code plugins from a marketplace on any surface you use, choose an install scope, and update or remove them later.

Installing a plugin adds its skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers to Claude Code on your machine.

This page is for anyone using plugins on their own machine or account, whether in the terminal, the desktop app, an IDE, or a cloud session: it covers installing, choosing a scope, adding marketplaces, and keeping plugins updated.

> [!NOTE]
>
> These cases are covered on other pages:
>
> * **You use claude.ai chat or Cowork, not Claude Code**: see [Plugins on claude.ai and in Cowork](https://claude.com/docs/plugins/overview)
> * **Claude Code printed an error**: find it in [Troubleshoot plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md)

Start with [Install a plugin](#install-a-plugin). If someone sent you an install command whose `@` name isn't `claude-plugins-official`, [add that marketplace](#add-a-marketplace) first.

## Install a plugin

As an example, this section installs [`commit-commands`](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/plugins/commit-commands) from [Anthropic's official marketplace](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/anthropic-marketplaces.md), which adds commands for committing, pushing, and opening pull requests.

The same steps install any other plugin: substitute its name and its marketplace's name wherever `commit-commands` and `claude-plugins-official` appear. If that plugin comes from a different marketplace, [add the marketplace](#add-a-marketplace) first.

Pick the tab for where you run Claude Code.

> [tab] Terminal
>
> Start Claude Code with `claude` in your project, then:
>
> **1. Open the plugin's details with the install command**
>
> Run `/plugin install` with the plugin's name and marketplace. In a session, this command doesn't install right away: it opens the `/plugin` panel on that plugin's details so you can review it and choose a scope first.
>
> ```text theme={null}
> /plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official
> ```
>
> To browse instead, run `/plugin` with no plugin name: the panel opens on the **Discover** tab, which lists the plugins from your marketplaces, and you can type to search, then press **Enter** on a plugin to open its details.
>
> **2. Review what the plugin adds**
>
> The details pane shows the plugin's description. It can also show:
>
> * **Will install**: the commands, agents, skills, hooks, and MCP and LSP servers the plugin adds.
> * **Last updated**: shown for a plugin in Anthropic's official marketplace.
> * **Context cost**: for a plugin in Anthropic's official marketplace, two token estimates. **Every turn** is what the plugin adds to each message you send, and **When invoked** is what its skills and agents add once Claude loads them. The estimates appear when you open the plugin by naming its marketplace, as the step 1 command does, or from the **Marketplaces** tab. The details pane you reach from the **Discover** list doesn't show them.
>
> Plugins from a local or custom marketplace can show `Components will be discovered at installation` instead.
>
> A plugin can run hooks and MCP servers, so read the pane before you install. See [Plugin security and trust](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/security.md).
>
> **3. Choose a scope**
>
> Select one of the three install options:
>
> * **Install for you (user scope)**: you get the plugin in every project on this machine
> * **Install for all collaborators on this repository (project scope)**: it's enabled for everyone who works in this repository
> * **Install for you, in this repo only (local scope)**: you get it in this repository only
>
> [Choose an install scope](#choose-an-install-scope) says which settings file each one writes to and which applies when the same plugin is set at more than one.
>
> After you select a scope, Claude Code installs the plugin along with any dependencies it declares, then prints an install summary.
>
> **4. Read the install summary**
>
> The last sentence of the summary tells you whether the plugin is usable in this session yet:
>
> * **Active now**: `Plugin is now active.` No reload is needed.
> * **Active, but a server needs setup**: `Plugin is now active.` is followed by `Its bundled MCP server needs configuration before it can start`. The plugin's [bundled MCP server](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/components.md#include-a-packaged-mcpb-server) can't start until you set its options. Select the plugin on the **Installed** tab in `/plugin` and choose **Configure** to set the server's options.
> * **Reload needed**: `Run /reload-plugins to apply.` The panel closes and Claude Code runs that reload for you. If the reload would [invalidate the prompt cache](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching.md#enabling-or-disabling-a-plugin), it warns and leaves the plugin pending instead. Run `/reload-plugins --force` to activate it anyway, which costs one uncached request.
> * **Load failed**: `The plugin couldn't be loaded`. Open the **Errors** tab in `/plugin` for the reason, then see [After install: plugin not working](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md#plugin-installed-but-not-working).
>
> **5. Confirm the plugin works**
>
> Type `/` and look for the plugin's skills under its name, in the form `/<plugin>:<skill>`. For `commit-commands`, `/commit-commands:commit` appears. Two other places list the plugin too:
>
> * Open the **Installed** tab in `/plugin`, which lists the plugin with its scope.
> * In your shell, run `claude plugin list`, which prints the same list with `Version`, `Scope`, and `Status` lines.
>
> If `/commit-commands:commit` doesn't appear, see [After install: plugin not working](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md#plugin-installed-but-not-working).
>
> Installing from any other marketplace requires one extra step first: [add the marketplace](#add-a-marketplace). Claude Code adds Anthropic's official marketplace for you the first time you start an interactive terminal session, which is why the example skips that step. If you found a plugin on [claude.com/marketplace](https://claude.com/marketplace), its **Claude Code** button copies the install command in its [shell form](#install-from-your-shell), `claude plugin install <name>@claude-plugins-official`.

> [tab] Desktop app
>
> In a local or SSH session in the desktop app's **Code** tab:
>
> **1. Open the plugin browser**
>
> Click the **+** button next to the prompt box and select **Add plugins**. If the **+** menu shows **Plugins** instead of **Add plugins**, select **Plugins**, then **Browse plugins**. The plugin browser opens with the plugins from your marketplaces.
>
> **2. Select the plugin**
>
> Find `commit-commands` and select it.
>
> **3. Choose a scope**
>
> Choose a [scope](#choose-an-install-scope): your user account, this project, or local-only.
>
> To enable, disable, or uninstall a plugin later, see [Install plugins in the desktop app](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop.md#install-plugins).

> [tab] VS Code
>
> In the Claude Code panel in VS Code:
>
> **1. Open Manage plugins**
>
> Type `/plugins` in the prompt box to open **Manage plugins**.
>
> **2. Install the plugin**
>
> On the **Plugins** tab, search for `commit-commands` and click **Install**. If the tab lists no plugins, add `anthropics/claude-plugins-official` on the **Marketplaces** tab first.
>
> **3. Choose a scope**
>
> Choose a [scope](#choose-an-install-scope): **Install for you**, **Install for this project**, or **Install locally**.
>
> Your changes apply to open sessions without a restart. See [Manage plugins in VS Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/vs-code.md#manage-plugins).

> [tab] Cloud session
>
> A [cloud session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments.md), including [the browser at claude.ai/code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md), has no plugin browser and doesn't load the plugins you installed on your own machine or the ones your repository's `.claude/settings.json` turns on. For plugins your organization distributes through managed settings, see [Manage plugins for your organization](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/org.md).
>
> See [which parts of your setup are also available in a cloud session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments.md#what-carries-over-from-your-setup) for the rest of your setup.

### Choose an install scope

A plugin's install scope decides who gets the plugin and which settings file records it as enabled:

* **User scope**: the plugin is enabled for you in every project on this machine. The entry goes in `enabledPlugins` in `~/.claude/settings.json`.
* **Project scope**: the plugin is enabled for everyone who works in this repository. The entry goes in `.claude/settings.json`, which you commit. Committing that entry turns the plugin on for your collaborators but doesn't download it to their machines. Each collaborator also runs `claude plugin install <name>@<marketplace> --scope project` once per clone; see [Enabled in project settings but not installed](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/loading.md#enabled-in-project-settings-but-not-installed).
* **Local scope**: the plugin is enabled for you in this repository only. The entry goes in `.claude/settings.local.json`.

Some plugins are set by their author to start turned off, through the [`defaultEnabled`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/manifest-reference#defaultenabled) field. Such a plugin is installed but stays off until you turn it on with `claude plugin enable <name>` in your shell, or from the **Installed** tab of `/plugin` in a session.

When the same plugin is set at several scopes, the local setting overrides the project setting, and the project setting overrides the user setting. See [Find where a plugin is enabled](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/loading.md#find-where-a-plugin-is-enabled) for the full rule.

The terminal, the desktop app's local sessions, and the VS Code extension on one computer read the same settings files, so a plugin you install at user scope in any of them is available in the other two.

### JetBrains, non-interactive runs, and the Agent SDK

Some places you run Claude Code have no plugin browser of their own:

* **JetBrains IDEs**: the JetBrains plugin runs Claude Code in the IDE's terminal, so use the **Terminal** tab's steps there.
* **`claude -p` and other non-interactive runs**: `/plugin` doesn't run, and Claude replies `/plugin isn't available in this environment.` Plugins you already installed do load. Install and manage them from your shell with [`claude plugin` commands](#install-from-your-shell).
* **Agent SDK**: load plugins through the SDK's plugin option. See [Load plugins in the Agent SDK](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/plugins.md).

If Claude Code reports that a plugin enabled in the repository's `.claude/settings.json` isn't installed, see [Enabled in project settings but not installed](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/loading.md#enabled-in-project-settings-but-not-installed).

> [!TIP]
>
> If you're a plugin author testing a copy of your plugin on disk, start Claude Code from your shell with `--plugin-dir` to load it for one session instead of installing it. See [Flags that load a plugin for one session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/cli-reference.md#flags-that-load-a-plugin-for-one-session).

### Plugins from your claude.ai account

Your claude.ai account is a separate source of plugins, alongside the marketplaces you install from:

* **What arrives**: every plugin you turn on for your claude.ai account, and every plugin your organization turns on for its members. In a terminal session they sync in the background each time you start Claude Code while signed in with that account; in Cowork sessions they download when the session starts.
* **Where you see them**: in `/plugin` and `claude plugin list` under the ID `<name>@synced`. You can turn one off at your own scope unless your organization requires it.
* **What doesn't go the other way**: plugins you install with `/plugin` or `claude plugin install` stay on this machine and aren't added to your claude.ai account.

For sync timing, sign-in requirements, and turning sync off, see [Plugins synced from claude.ai](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/loading.md#synced-plugins).

### Install from your shell

Run `claude plugin install` in your shell to install a plugin without starting a Claude Code session, for example from a setup script.

* **Scope**: user scope by default. Pass `--scope project` or `--scope local` to change it.
* **When the plugins load**: plugins it installs load the next time you start Claude Code, or when you run `/reload-plugins` in a session that's already open.
* **The marketplace on a new machine**: on a machine where no one has opened an interactive Claude Code session yet, the official marketplace isn't registered, so a script that installs from it runs `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official` before the install. See [Add and install from your shell](#add-and-install-from-your-shell).

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin install formatter@your-org --scope project
```

The command prints `Successfully installed plugin: formatter@your-org (scope: project)` when it finishes.

Some plugins install by running a command that their marketplace names, called a [`command` source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/marketplace-reference#command-plugin-source). Claude Code shows you that command and asks you to accept it before it runs. A script has no one to answer that prompt, so pass `--yes` there to accept it.

For the other `claude plugin install` flags, see [plugin install](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/cli-reference.md#plugin-install).

## Add a marketplace

You only need this section when the plugin you want isn't in Anthropic's official marketplace, for example one a coworker published or one from Anthropic's community marketplace.

A marketplace is a catalog of plugins, and Claude Code has to know about a marketplace before you can install from it. You add a marketplace once. After that, its plugins appear on the **Discover** tab and install with `/plugin install <plugin>@<marketplace>` in a session or `claude plugin install <plugin>@<marketplace>` in your shell, where `<marketplace>` is the name the marketplace registered under. To do both in one step, see [Add a marketplace and install in one command](#add-a-marketplace-and-install-in-one-command).

In a Claude Code session, run `/plugin marketplace add` followed by the marketplace's source: a GitHub repository, a git repository on any host, a local directory or file, or a hosted `marketplace.json`.

| Source | What you type | Example |
| :- | :- | :- |
| GitHub repository | `owner/repo`. Add `#ref` to pin a branch or tag. | `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official`, or `/plugin marketplace add your-org/plugins#v1.2.0` to pin the `v1.2.0` tag |
| Git repository on any host | The full clone URL. Add `#ref` to pin a branch or tag. | `/plugin marketplace add https://gitlab.example.com/your-group/your-marketplace.git#v1.0.0` |
| Local directory or file | A relative or absolute path to a directory that holds `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, or to the JSON file itself. Start a relative path with `./` or `../`, because Claude Code reads a bare `name/name` as a GitHub repository. | `/plugin marketplace add ./my-marketplace` |
| Hosted `marketplace.json` | Its `https://` URL | `/plugin marketplace add https://example.com/marketplace.json` |

From your shell, `claude plugin marketplace add` takes the same sources.

> [!TIP]
>
> `/plugin market` also works as a shorter form of `/plugin marketplace`.

Include the `https://` prefix on every URL, or use the `git@host:path` form for SSH. If you type a bare `gitlab.example.com/your-group/your-marketplace.git`, Claude Code reads it as GitHub `owner/repo` shorthand and rejects it.

When the command succeeds, it prints `Successfully added marketplace: <name>`, and the marketplace's plugins appear on the **Discover** tab the next time you open `/plugin`, with no reload needed. If it fails, match the error message in [Troubleshoot plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md#add-a-marketplace).

### Add a marketplace and install in one command

To install a plugin from a marketplace you haven't added yet, name the marketplace source with `--marketplace` on the install command, in a session or from your shell. The source takes [the same forms as `/plugin marketplace add`](#add-a-marketplace), such as GitHub `owner/repo`, a git URL, or a local path. Give the plugin name by itself, without an `@marketplace` suffix.

#### Add and install in a session

Run `/plugin install` in a Claude Code session with the plugin and the source. Requires Claude Code v2.1.275 or later. In a session, the source can't contain spaces.

```text theme={null}
/plugin install deploy-helper --marketplace your-org/plugins
```

If you haven't added that marketplace yet, Claude Code shows the source it resolved and asks you to confirm before adding it. Once the marketplace is added, the plugin's details open and you choose an [installation scope](#install-a-plugin). If the source matches a marketplace you've already added, Claude Code skips the confirmation and opens the plugin's details in that marketplace.

#### Add and install from your shell

In your shell, without starting a session, run `claude plugin install` with the plugin and the source. Requires Claude Code v2.1.292 or later.

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin install deploy-helper --marketplace your-org/plugins
```

The shell command adds the marketplace without a confirmation step. A marketplace you've already added from that source is reused. A new one is added under the same [organization policy checks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/org.md#restrict-what-users-can-install) as `claude plugin marketplace add`, and is declared in your user settings even when you pass `--scope project`.

If you haven't added that marketplace yet, the command prints `Successfully added marketplace: <name> (declared in user settings)` and then [installs the plugin](#install-from-your-shell).

### Add a private marketplace

A private marketplace is one in a repository you need credentials to clone, on GitHub or any other git host. You add it with the same `/plugin marketplace add` or `claude plugin marketplace add` command as a public one. Claude Code clones it with the git credentials already on your machine and never prompts, so each way of connecting has a requirement:

* **HTTPS**: your git credential helpers apply, so access you set up with `gh auth login`, the macOS Keychain, or `git-credential-store` works. Git's prompts and askpass programs are off, including one set in `GIT_ASKPASS`, so the clone fails instead of prompting when git would have to ask for a credential.
* **SSH**: the host must already be in your `known_hosts` file and the key must work without a passphrase prompt. If your git setup names an SSH program in `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, `GIT_SSH`, or your git config's `core.sshCommand`, Claude Code runs that program.
* **GitHub `owner/repo` shorthand**: Claude Code checks whether your SSH key authenticates to `github.com`, then clones over SSH if it does and over HTTPS if it doesn't. Set [`CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_PREFER_HTTPS=1`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#variables) to skip that check and always clone over HTTPS.

The same credentials apply when you run `/plugin install`, `/plugin marketplace update`, and `claude plugin update`.

On a GitHub Enterprise Server host, see [Plugin marketplaces on GHES](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-enterprise-server.md#plugin-marketplaces-on-ghes) for the credentials each operation needs.

If your organization registers the marketplace for you through managed settings, you don't add it yourself. See [Pre-install and require plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/org.md#pre-install-and-require-plugins).

### Add a marketplace from claude.ai

In terminal sessions where [plugins sync from your claude.ai account](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/loading.md#synced-plugins), claude.ai can also list plugin marketplaces for you, such as your organization's plugin library and your own claude.ai uploads. You add one of these by its name rather than by a source. Adding a marketplace from claude.ai requires Claude Code v2.1.273 or later.

Add a claude.ai marketplace from the `/plugin` panel or from your shell:

* **Inside a session**: run `/plugin` and go to the **Marketplaces** tab, which lists the marketplaces from claude.ai. Select one there to add it.
* **From your shell**: run `claude plugin marketplace list`, which prints them in a `From claude.ai:` section. Then run `claude plugin marketplace add` with the `--claudeai` flag and the name shown in the list.

For example, this command adds a marketplace named `claudeai-organization-library`:

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin marketplace add --claudeai claudeai-organization-library
```

Claude Code registers the marketplace under a local name that starts with `claudeai-`, derived from the name that claude.ai lists it under. For example, a marketplace listed as "Organization library" becomes `claudeai-organization-library`. Install its plugins by that name, for example with `claude plugin install <plugin>@claudeai-organization-library`.

If you sign out, or sign in to a different claude.ai organization, the marketplace stays configured but shows no plugins, and the plugins you already installed from it keep loading.

The `From claude.ai:` section can also list git-based marketplaces shared through claude.ai, and it prints a source for each of those. Add them by that source as in [Add a marketplace](#add-a-marketplace), not with `--claudeai`.

## Manage installed plugins

The **Installed** tab in `/plugin` lists your plugins with actions to enable, disable, update, or uninstall each one. In a Claude Code session, run `/plugin` and press **Tab** to reach it, or run `/plugin enable`, `/plugin disable`, or `/plugin uninstall` to open the panel and make that change there. Disabled plugins are grouped under a collapsed header at the bottom of the list. Use these keys on the list:

* Type to filter by name or description.
* Press **Space** to enable or disable the selected plugin, and **f** to favorite it.
* Press **Enter** to open a plugin's details.

A plugin's details menu offers **Disable plugin** or **Enable plugin**, **Update now**, and **Uninstall**. Two more items appear for plugins that take settings, and a plugin can show both:

* **Configure options**: shown when the plugin's manifest declares [`userConfig` options](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/manifest-reference#user-configuration). Opens the dialog for those options
* **Configure**: shown when the plugin includes a [bundled MCP server](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/components.md#include-a-packaged-mcpb-server). Sets that server's own `user_config` settings

The tab can also show plugins at **Managed** scope. Your organization installed those through [managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#settings-files), and you can't enable, disable, or uninstall them here.

For a synced plugin that your organization requires on claude.ai, see [Manage plugins synced from claude.ai](#manage-plugins-synced-from-claude-ai).

When you close the `/plugin` panel with pending changes you made in it, Claude Code runs `/reload-plugins` for you to apply them. If the reload would [invalidate the prompt cache](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching.md#enabling-or-disabling-a-plugin), it warns and leaves the changes pending instead. Run `/reload-plugins --force` to apply them anyway.

### Manage plugins synced from claude.ai

The **Installed** tab in `/plugin` also lists the [plugins synced from your claude.ai account](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/loading.md#synced-plugins), with `synced` as their source. Synced plugins appear in terminal sessions on Claude Code v2.1.273 or later.

* **Enable or disable**: use the **Installed** tab, unless your organization marked the plugin as required.
* **Remove**: turn the plugin off on claude.ai.

When Claude Code syncs an added, updated, or removed plugin into an interactive session, you see `Plugins changed. Run /reload-plugins to activate.` Run `/reload-plugins` to load the change in that session, or leave it for the next time you start Claude Code.

### Uninstall a plugin the project enables

When you choose **Uninstall** for a plugin that this repository's `.claude/settings.json` enables, whether from the **Installed** tab or with `/plugin uninstall`, Claude Code asks whether to disable it for you or uninstall it for everyone:

* **Disable for me**: press **y**. Claude Code writes `false` for the plugin in your `.claude/settings.local.json` and leaves it installed for the project.
* **Uninstall for everyone**: press **u**. Claude Code removes the plugin from the shared `.claude/settings.json`.

### See what an installed plugin adds to your sessions

In your shell, run `claude plugin details <name>` for an installed plugin. The `Always-on` line is the number of tokens the plugin adds to every session where it's enabled, and the per-component rows show which skill or agent contributes most. For the full output and what each figure means, see [Measure what a plugin costs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/measure.md#measure-what-a-plugin-costs).

### Find plugins you no longer use

On the **Installed** tab in `/plugin`, plugins you installed yourself and haven't used recently appear under a **Not used recently** header, and each plugin's details show a **Last used** line. Use that header and that line to find plugins that still add startup and context cost, then disable or uninstall them.

### Plugins with dependencies

A plugin can declare other plugins that it depends on. When you install, disable, or uninstall such a plugin from a marketplace, Claude Code acts on those dependencies too:

* **Install**: Claude Code also installs and enables the plugin's declared dependencies at the same scope. The success message lists them.
* **Enable**: Claude Code also enables the plugin's dependencies that are installed but disabled. If a declared dependency isn't installed, the enable fails and the message tells you to install it first.
* **Disable**: when another enabled plugin still needs the one you named, Claude Code refuses and prints a chained command that disables both in the right order.
* **Uninstall**: auto-installed dependencies stay until you run `claude plugin prune` in your shell; see [plugin prune](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/cli-reference.md#plugin-prune).

If you loaded the plugin with `--plugin-dir` instead, see [Test a plugin and its dependency locally](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/dependencies.md#test-a-plugin-and-its-dependency-locally).

### Manage plugins from your shell

You can also manage plugins without starting a Claude Code session. In your shell, run `claude plugin install`, `enable`, `disable`, or `uninstall` as ordinary terminal commands; they change the same settings the `/plugin` panel does. Each takes `--scope` to target one scope, and uses a default scope when you omit it:

* `enable` and `disable` act on the most specific scope whose settings already list the plugin.
* `install` and `uninstall` act on user scope.

For example, these commands disable and re-enable a plugin, then uninstall it at project scope:

```bash theme={null}
claude plugin disable formatter@your-org
claude plugin enable formatter@your-org
claude plugin uninstall formatter@your-org --scope project
```

## Keep plugins updated

Plugins update automatically when the marketplace they came from has auto-update turned on. After a session starts, Claude Code refreshes those marketplaces and updates the on-disk copies of the plugins you installed from them.

The running session keeps the versions it already loaded. After an update, you see `Plugin updated: <name> · Run /reload-plugins to apply`, and the next session loads the new versions automatically.

These are the auto-update defaults for each kind of marketplace:

* **On by default**: `claude-plugins-official` and the other [official marketplace names](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/security.md#official-marketplace-names) except `knowledge-work-plugins` and `first-party-plugins`, plus [marketplaces added from claude.ai](#add-from-claude-ai).
* **Off by default**: every other marketplace, including the community marketplace, third-party marketplaces, and local development marketplaces.

For when auto-update runs, which plugins it skips, and the environment variables that turn it off, see [When auto-update runs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/loading.md#when-auto-update-runs).

### Turn auto-update on or off for a marketplace

In a Claude Code session, run `/plugin` and go to the **Marketplaces** tab. Select the marketplace, then select **Enable auto-update** or **Disable auto-update**.

### Update plugins now

To update one plugin, open it on the **Installed** tab in `/plugin` during a session and select **Update now**, or run `claude plugin update <plugin>@<marketplace>` in your shell.

There's no command that updates every plugin at once. To update the plugins you installed from one marketplace at once, go to the **Marketplaces** tab in `/plugin`, select the marketplace, and choose **Update marketplace**. That refreshes the marketplace's listing, updates the plugins you installed from it, and reports any plugin it left for you to update yourself. A plugin with a [`command` source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/marketplace-reference#command-plugin-source) or with a marketplace entry that sets a `headersHelper` command isn't updated this way, so you update it from its view on the **Installed** tab or with `claude plugin update <plugin>@<marketplace>`.

If you run `claude plugin marketplace update` in your shell with no name, it refreshes every marketplace's listing but leaves your installed plugins at their current versions.

### Auto-update from a private marketplace

For a private marketplace, see [What background auto-update does with credentials](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/host-marketplace.md#what-background-auto-update-does-with-credentials) for how background auto-updates authenticate over SSH and HTTPS, and [Troubleshoot plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md#add-a-marketplace) for the messages you see when they fail.

## Manage marketplaces

The **Marketplaces** tab in `/plugin` lists every marketplace you registered, along with its source. Select one to browse its plugins, update its listing, turn auto-update on or off, or remove it.

You can also list, update, and remove marketplaces with commands, from your shell or inside a session:

| Action | In your shell | Inside a session |
| :- | :- | :- |
| List marketplaces | `claude plugin marketplace list` | `/plugin marketplace list` |
| Update a marketplace's listing | `claude plugin marketplace update <name>` | `/plugin marketplace update <name>` |
| Remove a marketplace | `claude plugin marketplace remove <name>` | `/plugin marketplace remove <name>` |

When you remove a marketplace, Claude Code uninstalls every plugin you installed from it and removes their `enabledPlugins` entries from your settings files. The **Marketplaces** tab names those plugins before it asks you to confirm.

## Next steps

* [Anthropic's marketplaces](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/anthropic-marketplaces.md): how the official and community marketplaces differ and where to browse each one
* [Plugin loading reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/loading.md): why a plugin loaded, didn't load, or didn't change after an update
* [Plugin security and trust](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/security.md): what to review before you install a plugin from a marketplace you don't know
* [Troubleshoot plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md): install and marketplace error messages with their fixes
* [Create a plugin](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/create.md): build your own
